# Pilot — Seattle and Chicago building permits (Socrata)

**Real data.** Generated by `tools/adapters/permits-socrata.py` from two live Socrata
portals, 60 permits each.

```bash
python3 tools/adapters/permits-socrata.py --city seattle --limit 60 --out examples/pilot-seattle-permits
python3 tools/adapters/permits-socrata.py --city chicago --limit 60 --out examples/pilot-chicago-permits
```

Two cities, because they differ in precisely the way the profile's disclosure stance was
written for: **Seattle publishes no applicant at all; Chicago publishes named private
individuals at their home addresses.**

## The optional-applicant decision was correct

The profile makes `applicant` optional, on the grounds that naming a private individual
against their home address is a disclosure decision the authority must take deliberately
rather than one the schema forces. Real data settles it.

Chicago's permits carry `contact_1_name` with a `contact_1_type`. Across 300 sampled
residential permits:

| contact type | count |
|---|---|
| OWNER AS GENERAL CONTRACTOR | 121 |
| OWNER | 32 |
| OWNER OCCUPIED | 15 |

Of the 32 typed `OWNER`, **17 are individual personal names**, published unmasked alongside a
residential street address. Seattle's dataset has no applicant field whatsoever and is a
perfectly conformant permit record without one.

Had `applicant` been required, Seattle could not have been represented at all — the same
failure `areaServed` produced against UK Contracts Finder — and every Chicago import would
have carried a private individual's name by default.

The adapter applies the profile's stance rather than merely documenting it: an applicant that
is clearly an organization is carried, one that looks like an individual is omitted and
counted. `--include-individuals` restores source fidelity. Of 60 Chicago permits, 40 applicant
organizations were carried and 15 individual names omitted, including some sole traders
(`ARCHITECT`, `ELECTRICAL CONTRACTOR`) — arguably over-cautious, but a sole trader's name is
still a personal name.

## Two checks needed calibrating, one caught a real error

**Caught a genuine source contradiction.** Seattle permit `6082745-CN` is recorded as issued
2010-03-17 and expiring **2008-10-24** — seventeen months earlier — with the description
*"Closed as Incomplete - Expired Permit"*. The check was right. A contradiction cannot be
published, so the adapter drops the impossible expiry and counts it rather than passing it
through or silently correcting it.

**Too absolute.** A permit marked `Completed` with a missing decision date was failing the
build. One Seattle record is a shoreline exemption with **all four dates null** — it asserts
nothing rather than asserting a completion while hiding when. The check now distinguishes
the two: partial dating is an error, no dating is a warning.

**An adapter fault, not a profile fault.** Seattle's `Closed` was mapped to `completed`, but
nine of eleven permits with no issue date are `Closed` — it means administratively closed, not
works signed off. Now mapped to `withdrawn`.

## Vocabulary drift is real

Chicago writes `PERMIT - SIGNS` with a hyphen and `PERMIT – EXPRESS PERMIT PROGRAM` with an
**en-dash**. Matching the literal string missed 42 of 60 permits. Permit vocabularies are
typed by hand and drift; the adapter normalises dashes and whitespace before lookup rather
than accumulating spelling variants — the same lesson the Legistar and CAP adapters taught.

## Coordinates

Both cities publish coordinates to 8–15 decimal places against residential addresses. The
adapter reduces to five — about a metre — consistent with the Open311 pilot, so a permit
locates a property rather than a point inside a house.
